newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Menem rallies party against Peronist enemies.
newsitem.headline: Menem rallies party against Peronist enemies.

text.p: President Carlos Menem, buffeted by falling polls and opposition to austerity moves, rallied his party on Thursday against "the enemy at the door" and evoked the ghost of the 1955 coup that overthrew party founder Gen. Juan Peron.

"We Peronists must stand together. The enemy is at the door and we must arm ourselves -- with truth and brotherhood," he said in an apppeal to Peronist lawmakers and governors for support for his flagging leadership.

In a speech eagerly awaited for signs he still has the political initiative despite strikes and problems persuading Congress to help him head off a $6.6 billion budget deficit, Menem urged the party faithful to be on the alert against any threat to the stability of his seven-year-old administration.

"I beg my brothers and sisters for us not to repeat the sad story of 1955, that Argentines never have to go through jail and torture again, that we don't lose the liberty we have conquered because of mere internal squabbles," Menem said.

His party bears little resemblance to that of the general whose populist rule lasted from 1946-55 and 1973-74, but modern-day Peronists still evoke Peron and his wife Eva. Peron's first period in power was ended in 1955 by a military coup supported by the oligarchy and the political opposition.
When Peron died in 1974 his third wife Isabel became president -- only to be toppled in 1976 by the military, who jailed Menem and many other Peronist leaders.
Polls show Menem's popularity at its lowest since he first came to power in 1989, despite just over a year having passed since he was reelected with 50 percent of the vote.

Trade unions, once loyal to Menem, are planning their second general strike in two months in late September to protest his austerity moves, his drive for more flexible labour laws and unemployment, which stands at 17.1 percent.

Menem said unions "are not going to scare me with strike threats" and accused the Radical and centre-left Frepaso opposition parties, who are planning a "black-out" protest in Buenos Aires on Sept. 12, of imitating previous protesters "who took the country to the brink of ruin".

The president reeled off the economic achievements of his government, including zero inflation versus 5,000 percent when he came to power, privatisations and currency stability since the peso was pegged to the U.S. dollar in 1991.

He pleaded for "strength, unity and solidarity so that Peronism keeps growing, because there are no other proposals in Argentina, no other proposals in Latin America, and the Argentine model is catching on in many parts of the world."

And while his Cabinet Chief Alberto Kohan told reporters that dissident Peronist governors and deputies who stayed away from the conclave could face sanctions, Menem called for "strength and unity" and promised "I won't let you down."
